#6171. Texas Democrats put DEI back on agenda after sweeping to power

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, discusses the 2026 midterm election results after Democrats flipped a Texas U.S. Senate seat and won the governor’s race on ‘Life, Liberty & Levin.’

Texas Democrats are opening their incoming state House majority with a push to clear the way for DEI offices and programs to return to public universities across the state — a move state Republicans are expected to block but that puts the culture-war issue front and center after massive Democratic Party gains in the state.

HB 358 and SB 125 would repeal a 2023 law banning diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) offices and programs at public universities, but the bills face steep odds with Republicans still retaining control of the Texas Senate. Still, the effort signals Democrats’ broader intent to roll back one of the GOP’s signature education policies after campaigning heavily on the war in Iran, immigration and affordability.

Even if the repeal effort fails, conservative policy experts in Texas warn that Democratic appointments to university governing boards could weaken enforcement of the state's DEI restrictions without changing the law.

"With Republicans in firm control of the Texas state Senate, it’s highly unlikely that any bill seeking to bring back the corrosive and wasteful higher ed DEI regime will make it to the Governor’s desk," Chuck DeVore, chief national initiatives officer for the Texas Public Policy Foundation (TPPF), told Fox News Digital. "What will likely happen is that relabeled and disguised DEI programs and classes will make a comeback over the next four years as the Governor’s board of regents appointees gradually get a majority. We look forward to suing to ensure adherence to Texas law."

FEDERAL JUDGE KICKED OFF 'BOTCH JOB' ANTI-DEI CASE AFTER STUNNING APPEALS COURT REBUKE

University of Texas students walk through campus on the first day of classes on Monday, Aug. 25, 2025. (Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

The 2023 anti-DEI law, signed by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, barred public universities from maintaining DEI offices or assigning employees or contractors to perform their duties. It also prohibited compelling or soliciting DEI statements from faculty or students, restricted certain preferences based on race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin and banned mandatory DEI training for students and employees. The law includes exceptions for academic instruction, scholarly research and registered student organizations.

After the law took effect Jan. 1, 2024, UT Austin closed its Multicultural Engagement Center and discontinued its Monarch program, which provided advising, mental-health support and scholarships to illegal immigrants and other noncitizen students. The University of Houston System stopped requiring DEI statements in hiring and promotions, while UT Health San Antonio ended a faculty loan-repayment program for professors from "underrepresented backgrounds."

VP VANCE TOUTS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S DISMANTLING OF DEI

At a May 2024 Texas Senate higher education subcommittee hearing, UT System Chancellor J.B. Milliken told lawmakers the system had closed 21 DEI offices, eliminated 311 full- and part-time positions focused on DEI and canceled 681 contracts, programs and training sessions. Critics have nevertheless accused some universities of preserving DEI initiatives under different names or organizational structures.

Texas A&M University drew scrutiny after dissolving its Office for Diversity but transferring six of its eight employees to other campus positions. Former Vice President for Diversity Annie McGowan received a 10% raise, a new position and nine months of paid leave. Critics accused the university of preserving DEI operations under different titles. Texas A&M maintained that the office and its DEI-related duties had been eliminated and that the raises were unrelated to DEI.

Activists hold signs during a news conference about diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) outside the U.S. Capitol on July 23, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Kate Bierly, a higher education campaign director at TPPF, told Fox News Digital that Democrats could undermine Texas' 2023 anti-DEI law without repealing it. She warned that newly appointed university regents could weaken enforcement through administrative inaction, potentially allowing prohibited practices to resume.

She observed that numerous university regents' terms expire Feb. 1, 2027, giving Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa an opportunity to nominate replacements who could influence how universities enforce the DEI ban.

CONGRESS TO PUT AMERICAN BAR ASSOCIATION IN HOT SEAT OVER DEI RULES TIED TO LAW SCHOOL ACCREDITATION

But Hinojosa would face another obstacle: Republican control of the Texas Senate, which must confirm university regent appointments. Bierly said the Texas Constitution allows certain unpaid gubernatorial appointees, including regents, to remain in office after their terms expire. Because the 90th Legislature convenes in January 2027, before the regents' terms expire, she said incumbents could remain in place until the end of the 91st Legislature's regular session in 2029 if their successors are not confirmed.

The State Capitol is seen in Austin, Texas, on June 1, 2021. (AP Photo/Eric Gay, File)

"If the Senate declines to confirm nominees who would undermine the state's DEI reforms, existing regents can continue serving rather than automatically surrendering their seats when their terms expire," Bierly said. "This holdover period ends on the last day of the first regular legislative session that begins after the term expires. So as a result, the current regents can hold over to 2029 if no successor has qualified by then. After that, the office becomes vacated."

DeVore said the holdover provision could become a political liability for Senate Republicans, giving Democrats "an actual useful campaign cudgel" if the chamber refuses to confirm Hinojosa's nominees. Democrats could accuse Republicans of obstructing the governor's appointments to university governing boards, he said.

That pressure could force a compromise at some point, DeVore added, but also warned that DEI is "a death issue for a Republican primary" and that any Republican who supports a compromise could be "toast in the primary."

State Representative Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat from Texas and then-gubernatorial candidate, speaks during a campaign event with State Representative James Talarico, a Democrat from Texas and U.S. Senate candidate, not pictured, at the Stubbs - Waller Creek Amphitheater in Austin, Texas, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR

Texas' restrictions reflect a broader national effort to dismantle DEI programs in government and higher education.

The Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling against race-based admissions preferences at universities preceded a broader federal crackdown on DEI. After returning to office in 2025, President Donald Trump moved to dismantle DEI programs across the federal government and directed federally funded schools to end race-based preferences in admissions, hiring, scholarships and other programs.

Republican-led states have pursued similar restrictions at public universities, making Texas’ fight part of a broader national backlash against institutional DEI.

Texas Democrats are opening their incoming state House majority with a push to clear the way for DEI offices and programs to return to public universities across the state. (fstop123/iStock via Getty Images Plus)

Texas' political landscape has shifted dramatically following Republican election losses. Abbott, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and Attorney General Ken Paxton are leaving office, while Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, lost his Republican Senate primary to Paxton.

Democrats won the governorship, attorney general's office and a U.S. Senate seat while reclaiming the state House for the first time in more than two decades. Republicans retained control of the state Senate, giving them a potential veto over both the DEI repeal legislation and Hinojosa's university regent nominees.

"Ultimately, Texas lawmakers must decide whether they want the DEI ban to be more than a law on paper," Bierly said. "Protecting the reforms requires attention not only to legislation, but also to the university leadership responsible for implementing it."

Fox News Digital sought comment from the repeal bills' sponsors, Democratic state Rep. John Bucy and Democratic state Sen. José Menéndez, as well as former Republican state Sen. Brandon Creighton, who authored the 2023 anti-DEI law and now serves as chancellor of the Texas Tech University System. None responded before publication. The University of Texas System, Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board and Texas Students for DEI also did not respond to requests for comment.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

#6170. 6 Reasons Why Citi Strata Elite Beats Amex Platinum And Sapphire Reserve

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Citi Strata Elite earns 50% more points on unbonused spending than Amex Platinum or Chase Sapphire Reserve, and those points can become American Airlines miles. It also costs $200 – $300 less per year.

I’ve written a lot about the card’s enormous first-year value. But the more I’ve used the hotel benefit, the more I think there’s a case for the Citi Strata EliteSM Card (See rates and fees) beyond the initial bonus. Here are six things it does better than Amex Platinum and Sapphire Reserve – both excellent cards and I have them both.

Banks advertise how many transfer partners they have. A long list can include many I even actively avoid (Aeromexico, Thai Airways). Most banks are also limited in whom they can work with because major airline and hotel cobrand card agreements usually include exclusivity provisions that limit what competing banks can offer. American Express has Delta. Chase has United. Citi has American. Of those three, I’d take American AAdvantage. Strata Elite points transfer to American at 1:1. And American still offers some terrific partner redemptions. However, some of my best American redemptions are just regular domestic coach trips. I’ve written about getting 4 cents and even 8 cents per mile from economy awards. American will sometimes make a flight cheap in miles while keeping the cash fare high. You don’t need to want a first class suite halfway around the world to get value from this program. Citi still has international partners I want, including Air France KLM Flying Blue, Singapore Airlines and Qatar Airways. Chase’s Hyatt transfers are a real advantage on the hotel side. (I still wish Bank of America had its own transferable points program, with Alaska’s Atmos Rewards as a partner.) 2. The Hotel Credit Works Beyond A Short List Of Luxury Properties Strata Elite offers up to $300 off prepaid hotel stays of two nights or longer booked through Citi Travel each calendar year. The discount comes off when you book, and applies to the room cost before taxes and fees. You can use it at ordinary hotels and independent properties, without restricting yourself to a luxury collection. Amex Platinum’s $600 annual hotel credit is split into two $300 periods and requires Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection bookings. Sapphire Reserve’s $500 The Edit credit is limited to that collection, with a maximum of $250 per qualifying booking. Chase also has an additional 2026 hotel credit, but that one is restricted to selected brands. Those programs can provide real value through breakfast, property credits and hotel loyalty benefits. Citi’s advantage is the much broader choice of hotels where I can use the discount. And I haven’t found that using Citi’s credit requires giving back the savings through a higher room rate. In January, I compared the Marriott at LaGuardia Airport: Citi Travel was $156 before taxes, while Marriott’s own member rate was $176. That’s $20 less per night before applying the credit. I still compare the room and cancellation terms, but Citi Travel has been competitive or even cheaper. I’ve also had little difficulty getting Marriott hotels to add my Bonvoy number at check-in and honor on-property benefits. Earlier this year I used the Strata Elite credit at a Marriott and received club lounge access. I similarly had no problem getting status recognition on a bank portal booking at a Westin this month. These third-party bookings generally aren’t supposed to be eligible for hotel points, elite-night credit or elite benefits. 3. It’s A Better Card For Everyday Spending Strata Elite earns 1.5 points per dollar on spending outside its bonus categories. Sapphire Reserve and Amex Platinum earn just one. You can do better with any bank pairing its primary card with a second card that offers different earn. Generally you’re permitted to pool those points. 4. Six Points Per Dollar On Weekend Evening Dining Is Fantastic Citi Nights earns six points per dollar at restaurants from 6 p.m. Friday until 6 a.m. Saturday, and again from 6 p.m. Saturday until 6 a.m. Sunday, all times Eastern. This works at restaurants generally, including qualifying restaurant delivery services. You don’t have to pick from a bank’s restaurant reservation list. Citi uses the time the purchase is authorized, so a Friday dinner doesn’t lose the bonus just because the charge posts on Monday. Outside Citi Nights, restaurant spending earns 3x. And Citi’s other big accelerators are 12x on hotels, car rentals and attractions booked through Citi Travel, and 6x on airfare booked there. You don’t earn points on the hotel spending covered by the $300 benefit. For airfare booked directly with an airline, Amex Platinum’s 5x and Sapphire Reserve’s 4x beat Citi’s 1.5x. Big Useful Credits Instead Of Many Small Ones I’ve laid out how to use the Strata Elite credits, but the basic approach is pretty simple: book a hotel stay and buy an American Airlines ticket. In addition to the $300 hotel benefit, there’s a $200 annual Splurge credit. Select American Airlines as one of your eligible merchants before purchasing, and a ticket billed directly by American qualifies. You don’t have to find incidental fees to use it on, as with Amex Platinum’s airline fee credit. The other choices are Best Buy, 1stDibs, Live Nation and Future Personal Training. You can activate up to two merchants at a time and use the credit over multiple eligible purchases. For me, American makes this easy. If the hotel benefit and Splurge credit replace $500 you’d have spent anyway, they leave just $95 of Citi’s $595 annual fee to cover. And both benefits run by calendar year, without dividing the money into monthly allowances. There’s also up to $200 a year for Blacklane, divided into $100 for January through June and $100 for July through December. 6. The Annual Fee Is Lower The annual fees are $595 for Citi Strata Elite vs $795 for Sapphire Reserve and $895 for Amex Platinum. You still get a premium travel card: Priority Pass lounge access with up to two guests, four Admirals Club passes each calendar year for eligible American or oneworld travel, travel protections, and up to $120 for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application every four years. And the first year still offers a lot. The current offer is 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 in the first three months. At 1.5 cents apiece, that’s $1,125 in points before counting what you earn from the spending itself. Someone opening the card now can use the hotel and Splurge benefits during the rest of 2026 and again in 2027, before their first anniversary. That’s up to $1,000 from those two benefits alone. If those credits replace spending you’d make anyway, the bonus plus the credits less the $595 fee comes to $1,530 in first-year value, before Blacklane, lounge access or points earned from purchases. Select American Airlines as one of your eligible merchants before purchasing, and a ticket billed directly by American qualifies. You don’t have to find incidental fees to use it on, as with Amex Platinum’s airline fee credit. The other choices are Best Buy, 1stDibs, Live Nation and Future Personal Training. You can activate up to two merchants at a time and use the credit over multiple eligible purchases. For me, American makes this easy. If the hotel benefit and Splurge credit replace $500 you’d have spent anyway, they leave just $95 of Citi’s $595 annual fee to cover. And both benefits run by calendar year, without dividing the money into monthly allowances. There’s also up to $200 a year for Blacklane, divided into $100 for January through June and $100 for July through December. 6. The Annual Fee Is Lower The annual fees are $595 for Citi Strata Elite vs $795 for Sapphire Reserve and $895 for Amex Platinum. You still get a premium travel card: Priority Pass lounge access with up to two guests, four Admirals Club passes each calendar year for eligible American or oneworld travel, travel protections, and up to $120 for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application every four years. And the first year still offers a lot. The current offer is 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 in the first three months. At 1.5 cents apiece, that’s $1,125 in points before counting what you earn from the spending itself. Someone opening the card now can use the hotel and Splurge benefits during the rest of 2026 and again in 2027, before their first anniversary. That’s up to $1,000 from those two benefits alone. If those credits replace spending you’d make anyway, the bonus plus the credits less the $595 fee comes to $1,530 in first-year value, before Blacklane, lounge access or points earned from purchases. While it would be a dream to get to every new hotel within days of opening to be among the first to experience special properties around the world, the reality is, that’s not always possible. When it is, though, you can bet we jump on the opportunity. Especially when it’s a flagship new points hotel.

That’s how I ended up staying at the gorgeous new Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur within a week of its opening on Oct. 30, 2026. To be clear, I understood that not all the hotel’s restaurants would be open, nor would its spa, so this is not a full review, rather a first glimpse at what’s sure to be a favorite Hilton points redemption option soon.

Although it’s the Malaysian capital’s newest hotel, the Waldorf Astoria actually occupies the site of the storied former Hotel Istana in the heart of city’s Golden Triangle district — so called because it is the capital’s main financial and shopping district, with luxury megamalls galore — which means it’s centrally located, but tucked onto a quiet stretch of Jalan Raja Chulan.

Because of that, the hotel feels secluded and quiet, but plugged into the rest of the city, and easily accessible to most of the activities international visitors are likely to seek out while in town.

The hotel feels like a destination unto itself, too, though, thanks to its palatial suites (no mere rooms here) and an impressive slate of bars and restaurants, including outposts from celebrity chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten and Bangkok-based Garima Arora. The hotel will also be home to Malaysia’s first and only La Prairie spa, and the outdoor pool is the perfect place to while away a tropical afternoon.

Here’s what else you should plan to do during your stay at the new Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur.

During my stay, only a fraction of the accommodations were ready for guests, but the hotel should be at full strength soon. There are no rooms here, just suites, which start at an impressive 80 square meters (861 square feet).

Deboss Collective is behind the decor, and sought inspiration from traditional Malay construction and crafts, incorporating lots of natural stone and timber, woven textiles and wooden furnishings that feel like contemporary urban updates to what you might find in a traditional rumah kampung, or village house.

To wit, there are huge windows overlooking the hotel grounds and the city skyline, letting in plenty of natural light. The carpet patterns and hardwood are meant to evoke traditional Malaysian marquetry while colorful accent walls call to mind vibrant Peranakan shophouses you can still find in parts of the city.

My suite’s footprint was enormous, with a huge, welcoming living area that included a 65-inch flatscreen television, a breakfast table which could double as a workdesk thanks to a panel of plugs, a rounded sofa and armchair and a low-slung wooden chair that blended colonial and midcentury influences.

In the separate bedroom, a king-size bed was dressed with crisp white sheets embroidered with a “WA,” just in case you forgot where you were. To either side were walls with a terete theme hearkening to the bamboo stalks that grow in gardens around the city. Another 55-inch flatscreen hung on the wall in there.

The bathroom was mostly white marble, including geometric floor tiling, but the countertops were a handsome darker hue. Anchoring the entire space was an elliptical standalone tub with a scalloped shell, while a water closet and separate walk-in shower stood close by. To lend a sense of place, the bath products are from Jo Malone’s Jo Loves line and scented with citrusy-fresh pomelo, which is a staple in Malaysian cuisine.

Considering this was a standard category room, it felt positively palatial, with a huge amount of real estate that provided a variety of distinct spaces to enjoy within the suite at different times.

The Waldorf Astoria isn’t the biggest hotel in town, but it fields an outsize roster of restaurants that should be a draw for guests and Kuala Lumpur locals alike.

You can’t call your hotel a Waldorf Astoria if it doesn’t have a version of Peacock Alley, the famous lobby lounge from the New York City original. The one here sits smack dab at the hotel entrance and has soaring ceilings, sculptural marble columns, dramatic overhead chandeliers and a variety of seating vignettes that feel homey yet upscale.

The all-day menu offers items like chicken skewers with lemongrass and coriander ($10.50), a Waldorf salad ($14.50), a smash burger ($22) and Malaysian nasi goreng ($17) among other options.

Named after the previous hotel to occupy this spot, Istana is the hotel’s all-day dining restaurant and is adjacent to the lobby. Breakfast includes an extensive buffet and both Western and Asian dishes. For lunch and dinner, you’ll find specialties like spiced Borneo chicken wings with a honey glaze ($10.50), chargrilled red snapper with wild ginger chili sambal ($23.75) and fresh fiddlehead ferns from the Cameron Highlands sauteed in coconut milk with tongue-torching bird’s eye chili ($8.75).

If you’re up for it, the durian dessert with coconut cream and a palm sugar compote and served with toasted buttery buns is a rich way to end the evening ($12).

This is Vongerichten’s farm-to-table concept, so you’ll find a menu focused on seasonal fruits and vegetables. The signature eggplant dip is smoky and smooth with tangy coconut yogurt and tomato chutney served with fluffy pita ($9.75). There are also tartines like a king crab crostini with tart lemon aioli and dill ($16.50), various pizzas and pastas, and an array of plant-based dishes including pistachio-crusted broccoli with hazelnut vinaigrette ($14.50).

At the entrance to ABC Kitchens KL, there is a bright, casual area with a cocktail bar and small plates.

Jean-Georges Vongerichten has a longstanding relationship with the Waldorf Astoria brand, so it should be no surprise that the signature restaurant here is a French-Malaysian fine-dining fusion restaurant courtesy of the chef. It is only open for dinner Tuesday-Saturday. I did not have the opportunity to dine here, but the menu features an entire caviar section, starters like diver scallops with caramelized cauliflower and caper-raisin emulsion ($29.50) and spice-charred duck breast with roasted cabbage and chili-lime broth ($39.50).

It was not yet open during my stay, but Yaari will be the hotel’s sophisticated Indian restaurant and will only be open for dinner from Wednesday-Sunday. The chef is Garima Arora, whose Bangkok restaurant, Gaa, holds two Michelin stars.

Located on the fourth floor, Coda feels like a swanky hideaway for those in the know. Glossy dark stone surfaces and emerald-green velvet chairs and banquettes give the space a swanky vibe, as does the menu of libations inspired by various vinyl albums, one of which will likely be spinning on the record player during your visit.

Even the classics get a Malaysian twist, like an old fashioned crafted with jerky-like beef bak kwa-washed Michter’s bourbon, cardamom, clove and cascara distillate and mandarin-infused jaggery for a sweet finish ($20.50).

Here are some of the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur’s other amenities:

Nightly rates at the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur start at around $520 or 100,000 Hilton Honors points.

The Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur is part of  American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts, so if you have or , you can make a booking through amextravel.com and receive perks like availability-based upgrades, up to a $100 credit to use on-property during your stay for things like drinks or meals, complimentary daily breakfast for two and guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout.

Both cards now offer a biannual $300 (up to $600 per calendar year) statement credit on prepaid stays at Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts, so you could save $300 on a reservation at the hotel if you are able to take advantage of one of these cards’ credits. Just note that this benefit is changing in 2027 and will require cardholders to book two nights or more to take advantage of the credit.

Related: Our favorite American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts around the world

All public areas at the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur are wheelchair-accessible thanks to elevators (with wheelchair-height buttons), ramps and wide pathways. The hotel has accessible rooms in the King Urban Deluxe category. These accommodations feature audio and visual alarms, an automatic door closer, and wheelchair-height door viewer.

The Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur is an exciting new points option in the Malaysian capital, and one with plenty of award availability. While 100,000 points is a lot to pay, considering the sheer size of the suites here and the relatively high (for Kuala Lumpur) price point, it might be well worth it. Once the hotel’s restaurants and spa are all open and operational, this should become one of the city’s most popular luxury hotels.

#6166. U.S. Pilot Arrested At London Heathrow Airport, Admits Cocaine Possession—Passengers Owed Over $150,000 Compensation

A 64-year-old U.S. pilot arrested at London Heathrow has pleaded guilty to possessing cocaine. Wayne Sigler, from Louisiana, was remanded in custody and faces two additional charges involving alleged drunkenness or unfitness for duty. According to the BBC’s report of information confirmed by the Metropolitan Police, Sigler was arrested on Sunday, November 1. He appeared in court on Saturday, November 7, and pleaded guilty to possessing cocaine. His next hearing is scheduled for December 7 at Isleworth Crown Court. Those charges fall under the Railways and Transport Safety Act 2003. The law also covers preparing to fly, duties after reporting for work, and standby. The charges don’t establish that he flew passengers while impaired. Reporting on the incident doesn’t identify the airline or flight, and I can’t directly confirm this is the right individual but there’s a Wayne Sigler who identifies as an American Airlines pilot in federal campaign donation records, and online discussion pegs him as an American pilot who came to the airline via America West and US Airways. On November 1, American Airlines 39 to Miami and American AIrlines 91 to Chicago O’Hare were both cancelled, and American 85 to O’Hare departed nearly 5 hours late. What Delayed Passengers Are Owed A flight departing Heathrow is covered by U.K. passenger compensation rules regardless of where the airline is based. For a journey over 3,500 kilometers, such as London to the U.S., a qualifying arrival delay of more than four hours means £520 per person (~ US$690.42). A three-to-four-hour delay falls into the £260 band. An airline can avoid the compensation payment when extraordinary circumstances caused the disruption. But the U.K. Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Lipton v BA Cityflyer rejected that defense in the case of a pilot’s illness. And paragraph 170 specifically addresses a pilot who drinks enough to be unfit to report for work. If that causes a cancellation, the court says the reason is “inherent in the airline’s activity and operations.” A plane with 250 passengers at £520 each would mean £130,000 in compensation or $172,500. There was a British Airways pilot who bragged about using cocaine during a Johannesburg layover. A flight attendant reported his messages, he was kept from operating the return flight, and the airline fired him. According to the BBC’s report of information confirmed by the Metropolitan Police, Sigler was arrested on Sunday, November 1. He appeared in court on Saturday, November 7, and pleaded guilty to possessing cocaine. His next hearing is scheduled for December 7 at Isleworth Crown Court.

Those charges fall under the Railways and Transport Safety Act 2003. The law also covers preparing to fly, duties after reporting for work, and standby. The charges don’t establish that he flew passengers while impaired.

Reporting on the incident doesn’t identify the airline or flight, and I can’t directly confirm this is the right individual but there’s a Wayne Sigler who identifies as an American Airlines pilot in federal campaign donation records, and online discussion pegs him as an American pilot who came to the airline via America West and US Airways.

On November 1, American Airlines 39 to Miami and American AIrlines 91 to Chicago O’Hare were both cancelled, and American 85 to O’Hare departed nearly 5 hours late.

#6165. Flight Attendants Union Chief Targets Regional Pay, Delta, and Worker Data

Photo Credit: Sara Nelson, Association of Flight Attendants' International President, at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York City on November 12, 2026.  Skift

The era of catch-up flight attendant raises is ending, but airlines shouldn’t expect labor costs to ease. The next fights are over regional pay and worker data.

Flight attendants and pilots saw massive pay jumps in recent negotiations. Association of Flight Attendants International President Sara Nelson doesn’t expect a repeat.

“I don’t think that we’re going to see the kind of increases that we saw this last time again, unless the industry turns around. Unless we have peace on Earth and everything is going swimmingly,” Nelson said Thursday at the Skift Aviation Forum.

The last wave of contracts was effectively the first real bargaining since 9/11, according to Nelson, and followed years of bankruptcies, mergers, and pandemic delays that left contracts “four, five, six years late.”

Now, the union wants smaller, more regular raises through more frequent bargaining and is turning to new fights: the pay gap at regional airlines, its

Association of Flight Attendants International President Sara Nelson told the Skift Aviation Forum that the record pay increases won in the last bargaining round are unlikely to repeat. Nelson said that round was effectively the first real bargaining since 9/11, coming after years of bankruptcies, mergers, and pandemic delays that left contracts four to six years late. With mainline contracts at carriers like American and United "pretty much buttoned up," Nelson said the union now wants smaller, more regular raises through more frequent bargaining, and is shifting its attention to three fights: pay at regional carriers such as PSA Airlines and Endeavor Air, where she said flight attendants earn roughly half of mainline pay while based in high-cost cities like Chicago and New York; its organizing campaign at Delta, the only major U.S. airline without unionized flight attendants, which Nelson said is "really close" with a 52% increase in activists since January; and worker data protections, modeled on the union's objections to Google's bankruptcy auction win for Spirit's employee data. Nelson also said boarding pay, now standard at most major U.S. carriers, will be defended in future talks: "The public is on our side. So there's no way they're going to claw that back."

#6164. California City Approves Protections for Polyamorous Arrangements

Nobody could have seen this coming, except all the conservatives who said it would happen.

Then-mayor of West Hollywood Chelsea Lee Byers attends the Stonewall Democratic Club’s 50th-anniversary celebration in West Hollywood, Calif., November 15, 2025.

Wilbert Roberts/Getty Images for Connor Treacy

The West Hollywood City Council unanimously approved an ordinance that allows multi-partner relationships (like a so-called throuple) to formally register as a domestic relationship and receive certain legal protections at the local level, such as visitation rights in jail and rental privileges. A “multi-partner relationship,” per the ordinance, requires that the individuals involved share “the common necessities of life,” are over age 18, are competent enough to enter a contract, are all participating consensually, are “responsible for one another’s welfare,” and are not related by blood or a member of an already declared partnership. There is no expressed limit to the number of individuals who may be involved in a recognized multi-partner relationship, and people living outside the city can register their relationship.

The idea of protections for polyamory was brought to Councilmember Chelsea Lee Byers last year by Christina Fialho, an attorney who founded the “Rewrite the BiLine” organization that “reshape[s] cultural norms and drive[s] policy change” through media narratives to “advance health equity, economic opportunity, and civil rights for bi+ people and non-nuclear families.” Fialho told the Los Angeles Times that “this law is just the beginning. . . . I think it makes it possible for people to dream about a future they once thought was out of reach.” According to public records, the city council deemed it “necessary” to recognize “diverse relationship structures,” such as those involving more than two adults, because they are “becoming increasingly common.” The city frames the ordinance as an anti-discrimination measure with symbolic value:

Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

#6163. Rail To The Austin Airport Is Back On The Table—After Costs Soared And A Voter Bait-and-Switch

Austin’s airport used to be super convenient but it’s outgrown itself. There are just too many passengers for the size of the facility, at peak times it can be nearly body to body as you navigate through the terminal. What was once curb-to-gate in minutes, security wait times on peak travel days can be quite long. And traffic gets backed up heading into and out of the airport. There’s a long trek across the road and through a parking garage, up and down levels, to get to Uber or taxis. They’re building a new terminal and a new headhouse. The airport’s solution is to get (a lot) bigger. It will never recapture the ease of a smaller airport, and it’s going to mean more walking and showing up even earlier. One thing Austin doesn’t have is rail to the airport. Voters approved higher property taxes in 2020 to pay for it, but the cost of the project ballooned and train ambitions remained – but the airport connection got axed to save money. Now the mayor wants to start the process of planning again for a train to the airport. The much smaller light rail system now being developed will cost nearly double what was once estimated, even though it won’t reach the airport when it’s supposed to open in 2033. But since the airport is building an entirely new face to the facility, it makes sense to plan for how a train would approach and where the station would go. Plus, they’re going to be looking to have the airport pay for a portion of it. That’s part of what the mayor means when he talks about rail reaching the airport without new tax money. Mayor Kirk Watson lays out a three-mile extension of the planned train, mostly elevated, with a station at the airport. He says the Federal Transit Administration has agreed to a streamlined environmental review, and the next nine to twelve months will be spent working through costs and funding. His challenge is to deliver it “within our existing budget approved by voters – no new taxpayer dollars.” Latest #WatsonWire: It’s time to start the process to get rail to the airport. For years, our Austin Bergstrom International Airport (ABIA or AUS) operated beyond the capacity it was originally designed to accommodate. That’s a sign of success, and a reminder that we can’t build Austin’s future relying on infrastructure designed for its past. We need to envision a successful future and prepare for it. The “Journey With AUS” expansion project is delivering significant improvements in building the kind of airport a growing, globally connected city like Austin needs for decades to come. As we build a better airport, we also need to think about how we’re going to get people there to catch their flights and how to get them out of there to participate in our city. A world-class airport needs a multimodal, world-class transportation system to connect to it. Sure, we need to improve roadway access. And we also should give people more choices about how they travel. We need to have the same long-term vision for Austin light rail that we’ve had for ABIA. An airport rail connection has been part of Austin’s long-term transportation vision for years. With Journey with AUS, we have a chance to plan these projects strategically rather than trying to connect them after the fact. Until now, Austin Transit Partnership (ATP) has appropriately prioritized navigating the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) process for phase 1 of our system. This year, ATP received the important Record of Decision (ROD) from FTA and completed, in record time, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process for phase 1. In addition to getting the ROD and completing the NEPA process, I’ve wanted all major design and construction contracts in place and assurance that all of our financial decision-making is guided by a financial stewardship protocol before ATP takes any other big next steps. We have the ROD, the NEPA process is complete, the major contracts are in place, and the financial stewardship protocol is being followed. With these important milestones met, we can now take a major step: ATP will start the planning activities for a potential extension to take Austin light rail all the way to the airport. Read more: https://t.co/JTYqnnRyEE — Mayor Kirk Watson (@KirkPWatson) November 10, 2026 Airport Rail Was Part Of What Voters Were Sold Austin rejected rail proposals in 2000 and 2014. The successful 2020 vote for a $7.1 billion project came when voters were home during the pandemic and governments were spending unprecedented sums on Covid relief. The city’s election explainer lays out a Blue Line running through downtown to the airport, an Orange Line connecting north and south Austin, and a downtown tunnel. There were also commuter rail and bus improvements, plus $300 million for housing intended to ‘prevent displacement’ along the transit corridors. The ballot itself pitched airport rail. Voters approved an additional 8.75 cents per $100 of taxable property value, described as $437.50 a year on a home with $500,000 of taxable value, with federal funding expected to cover about 45% of the cost. Then the rail cost estimate exploded. By 2022, the original rail component had gone from $5.8 billion to $10.3 billion. That was blamed on inflation, land costs and construction costs but it was also the result of design changes to add more undeground tunneling. Without enough money, the connection out to the airport was dropped. The train got chopped from 20 miles to 9.8 miles. 26 stations down to 15 It lost airport servic and a downtown subway And the cost went from $5.8 billion to $8.2 billion With opening delayed from a planned 2029 reaching the airport to 2033 without it. The airport got dropped from ‘phase one’ and became labeled a ‘preferred priority extension’ if additional funding materialized. Now The Idea Is To Have The Airport Pay For Part Of It The Mayor repeatedly connects the rail extension to the airport’s ‘Journey With AUS’ expansion program. Austin is rebuilding its terminal frontage, roads and parking arrangements. And it’s building a new concourse. This is when you want to reserve space for a rail station. Journey With AUS uses airport revenues, airport revenue bonds, passenger facility charges and federal aviation grants. The airport sold $1.18 billion in May and plans $4.2 billion more through 2030. That money is spoken for, but the city owns the airport and it generates tremendous revenue. There are limits on what it can do with the money – the federal government makes grants and doesn’t want that money diverted. However, In 2021, the FAA began allowing on-airport rail infrastructure to receive airport funding even when the broader line serves people who aren’t using the airport. And 2025 FAA guidance says airports can contribute to ground access projects, including facilities beyond airport the property, provided airport funds support the airport-related share. So the airport link can open up airport funds now, as well as avoiding duplicate construction. The mayor frames the effort as “no new taxpayer dollars” but that’s different from “no new airport dollars” and the airport is owned by taxpayers. The Rail System’s Financing May Be Illegal, But The Election Could Change That The city created a separate public nonprofit corporation to pay for the train, so that the city itself wouldn’t be the one incurring debt. Then it held an election about the property tax rate, instead of one authorizing the city to borrow a specified amount of money. The city collects the property taxes and transfers the money to the special corporation which issues and pays interest on the bonds. Normally, in Texas, the city would have to specify an amount of debt to raise. If they later wanted to take on more debt, they’d have to go back to voters. Instead, they raised taxes by a specified amount and dedicated that tax stream to the project. Basically the city isn’t issuing the bonds, and isn’t taking on debt. The city also says it transfers the money each year, but future city councils could just stop making the transfers (winky, winky). There’s no city debt so they didn’t have to follow state rules for the city issuing debt. So property taxes support the borrowing, but the city isn’t mkaing a binding multiyear promise. There’s no debt. The state’s attorney general said this was completely illegal and sued. But he ran for Senate. After being impeached for corruption. This is the guy who spent the nation’s 250th birthday outside the country on vacation with the girlfriend he cheated on his wife (a state senator!) with. And he was videotaped partying in Dubai with fugitives. So he lost, along with every other Republican running for statewide office. It’s unclear whether the new attorney general will drop the case. For now, whether the state can take a tax increase and use it in perpetuity for a project that has ever-increasing capital costs, and then pivot later to use the funds to subsidize operations, remains tied up in the courts. There’s also a citizen lawsuit over the project’s bait and switch. Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for. For years, our Austin Bergstrom International Airport (ABIA or AUS) operated beyond the capacity it was originally designed to accommodate. That’s a sign of success, and a reminder that we can’t build Austin’s future relying on infrastructure designed for its past.

We need to envision a successful future and prepare for it.

The “Journey With AUS” expansion project is delivering significant improvements in building the kind of airport a growing, globally connected city like Austin needs for decades to come.

As we build a better airport, we also need to think about how we’re going to get people there to catch their flights and how to get them out of there to participate in our city.

A world-class airport needs a multimodal, world-class transportation system to connect to it. Sure, we need to improve roadway access. And we also should give people more choices about how they travel.

We need to have the same long-term vision for Austin light rail that we’ve had for ABIA.

An airport rail connection has been part of Austin’s long-term transportation vision for years. With Journey with AUS, we have a chance to plan these projects strategically rather than trying to connect them after the fact.

Until now, Austin Transit Partnership (ATP) has appropriately prioritized navigating the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) process for phase 1 of our system. This year, ATP received the important Record of Decision (ROD) from FTA and completed, in record time, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process for phase 1.

In addition to getting the ROD and completing the NEPA process, I’ve wanted all major design and construction contracts in place and assurance that all of our financial decision-making is guided by a financial stewardship protocol before ATP takes any other big next steps.

We have the ROD, the NEPA process is complete, the major contracts are in place, and the financial stewardship protocol is being followed.

With these important milestones met, we can now take a major step: ATP will start the planning activities for a potential extension to take Austin light rail all the way to the airport.

Austin is rebuilding its terminal frontage, roads and parking arrangements. And it’s building a new concourse. This is when you want to reserve space for a rail station. Journey With AUS uses airport revenues, airport revenue bonds, passenger facility charges and federal aviation grants. The airport sold $1.18 billion in May and plans $4.2 billion more through 2030. That money is spoken for, but the city owns the airport and it generates tremendous revenue. There are limits on what it can do with the money – the federal government makes grants and doesn’t want that money diverted. However, In 2021, the FAA began allowing on-airport rail infrastructure to receive airport funding even when the broader line serves people who aren’t using the airport. And 2025 FAA guidance says airports can contribute to ground access projects, including facilities beyond airport the property, provided airport funds support the airport-related share. So the airport link can open up airport funds now, as well as avoiding duplicate construction. The mayor frames the effort as “no new taxpayer dollars” but that’s different from “no new airport dollars” and the airport is owned by taxpayers. Then it held an election about the property tax rate, instead of one authorizing the city to borrow a specified amount of money. The city collects the property taxes and transfers the money to the special corporation which issues and pays interest on the bonds. Normally, in Texas, the city would have to specify an amount of debt to raise. If they later wanted to take on more debt, they’d have to go back to voters. Instead, they raised taxes by a specified amount and dedicated that tax stream to the project. Basically the city isn’t issuing the bonds, and isn’t taking on debt. The city also says it transfers the money each year, but future city councils could just stop making the transfers (winky, winky). There’s no city debt so they didn’t have to follow state rules for the city issuing debt. So property taxes support the borrowing, but the city isn’t mkaing a binding multiyear promise. There’s no debt. The state’s attorney general said this was completely illegal and sued. But he ran for Senate. After being impeached for corruption. This is the guy who spent the nation’s 250th birthday outside the country on vacation with the girlfriend he cheated on his wife (a state senator!) with. And he was videotaped partying in Dubai with fugitives. So he lost, along with every other Republican running for statewide office. It’s unclear whether the new attorney general will drop the case. For now, whether the state can take a tax increase and use it in perpetuity for a project that has ever-increasing capital costs, and then pivot later to use the funds to subsidize operations, remains tied up in the courts. There’s also a citizen lawsuit over the project’s bait and switch. Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for. Austin rejected rail proposals in 2000 and 2014. The successful 2020 vote for a $7.1 billion project came when voters were home during the pandemic and governments were spending unprecedented sums on Covid relief.

The city’s election explainer lays out a Blue Line running through downtown to the airport, an Orange Line connecting north and south Austin, and a downtown tunnel. There were also commuter rail and bus improvements, plus $300 million for housing intended to ‘prevent displacement’ along the transit corridors. The ballot itself pitched airport rail.

Voters approved an additional 8.75 cents per $100 of taxable property value, described as $437.50 a year on a home with $500,000 of taxable value, with federal funding expected to cover about 45% of the cost.

Then the rail cost estimate exploded. By 2022, the original rail component had gone from $5.8 billion to $10.3 billion. That was blamed on inflation, land costs and construction costs but it was also the result of design changes to add more undeground tunneling. Without enough money, the connection out to the airport was dropped.

Back in 2016 when I first started traveling to Austin frequently, the airport was one of the easier destinations to get in and out of. Then they moved Uber and Lyft to the remote parking lot 4 city blocks from the terminal doors and causing you to have drag your baggage upstairs, or downstairs to get to the pickup area depending on what level you exited the terminal. Not very convenient at all, and now, it has become very congested at times and all of the eating establishments and concessions are basically overrun at lunch, dinner, and breakfast. I hope they do the rebuild right.

The fundamental problem with light-rail systems is simple: How do people get from their homes to a rail stop?

If they have to drive (and park) there, they may as well just drive the rest of the way to their destination.

“ Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for.”

It’s quite common that driving & parking at a rail station then taking the train is far faster & cheaper than driving & parking at a major destination (such as an airport).

Voters never learn that transit systems always cost several times the original estimates while delivering less than promised. Austin’s results are nevertheless better than LAX’s people mover, let alone California’s high speed rail money pit. I thought that Oakland wasted $800 million on a BART connector to replace shuttle buses, but later projects are almost making that look like a bargain.

Too many make the mistake of believing the progressives when they say they want rail service to anywhere. They don’t really care if a single foot of track is ever laid down or not They only purpose of the rail projects is to siphon billions of dollars from taxpayers to well connected progressive companies and NGO’s. True in CA and LAX, and will be the same in Austin.

As they say history repeats itself. When SeaTac made it’s first renovation, it was more important to build parking garage adjacent to terminal then a light rail station. When light rail finally started is was projected so far over budget that federales were going pull funding. The City went back to taxpayers who swallowed and said ok. So, you can now take the light rail downtown to the airport painlessly(until you pay taxes on it).

Now, you can get on as far north as Lynwood(Everett planned). Also, you can go from UW to airport. And within the past year, you can go to and from Bellevue and Redmond(Microsoft hq). And that is a first by light rail over the Lake Washington floating bridge. A world’s first. So Gary, it only costs an unbelievable amount of taxpayer money.

The real issue with light rail (which nobody likes to talk about but is the #1 issue) is personal safety. The reality with most light rail systems (particularly at night but in some cities 24/7) is that there’s often a not-insignificant probability that you will be mugged, raped, or murdered. For the majority of people with the means to avoid light rail, they will do so, just like they avoid buses for the same reason. Just ask Iryna Zarutska.

RE: TexasTJ. LOL. I remember doing miles runs for early flights at JFK. When I got on the A train at around 4 AM, it was like a homeless hotel. I was like the only non-homeless on the train. I tried to find an empty place to sit. I was never robbed or assaulted, unless one considers unwashed odor as assault.

Also, I never actually missed a flight due to train stoppages. But I was always afraid I would.

However, I think the discussion about trains is kind of a red herring. The topic of the article, I think is about politician can handing out contracts and pay a lot of city workers on a train project. That is politicians are treating a train project as a loop-hole in the “no city debt” rules.

Kevin Jackson, President, Porter AirlinesArjan Meijer, President, Embraer Commercial Aviation

Moderated by Meghna Maharishi, Airlines Reporter, Skift

Airlines choosing new aircraft must weigh lower per-seat operating costs against the revenue consequences of deploying more capacity than a market can support. Business-class fliers on United Airlines will soon be able to relax in a fancy new Polaris Lounge at Denver International Airport (DEN).

Design work is underway on the new, exclusive lounge at DEN, Aaron McMillan, the managing director of hospitality programs at United, told TPG on Monday.

“We’re going to build a mezzanine on top of [the existing] mezzanine and expand the floor plate a little bit,” he said referring to a location at DEN near the end of Concourse A between gates A18 and A20. “We’ll have a two-story Polaris lounge there.”

United aims to open the new DEN Polaris Lounge by late 2028 or early 2029, added McMillan.

The news comes amid a club building spree by the airline. United opened a massive Washington, D.C.-inspired United Club in the new E Concourse at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) on Tuesday. The space is second in size only to the new club at Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) that opened in October.

United is also building a new club at San Francisco International Airport (SFO) that is scheduled to open by the end of the year, and is in talks for new clubs at Southwest Florida International Airport (RSW) in Fort Myers and Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC).

The Polaris Lounge is United’s premium airport space accessible only to fliers booked in same-day, long-haul business class or in business or first class on several partner airlines, including All Nippon Airways (ANA) and Lufthansa.

The spaces compete with American Airlines’ Flagship Lounges and Delta Air Lines’ Delta One Lounges.

United has six Polaris Lounges: Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), IAH, Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), SFO and IAD.

DEN is United’s only mainland U.S. hub without a Polaris Lounge.

When United opened its first Polaris space at ORD in 2016, lounges were only planned at its main international gateways and not DEN. The Colorado hub boasted only one long-haul nonstop at the time: Tokyo’s Narita Airport (NRT), schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

Today, United flies five intercontinental routes from DEN: Frankfurt Airport (FRA), London’s Heathrow Airport (LHR), Munich Airport (MUC), Rome Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO) and NRT. It will add its sixth route, to Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), next summer.

“Aside from the local departures we’ve grown out of Denver, there’s also a fairly significant number of local customers that are connecting over like Chicago, and Houston, and San Francisco that are traveling Polaris that can take advantage of the product,” said McMillan.

And while McMillan was mum on the look and feel of the new Polaris Lounge at DEN, he was confident in one thing: it will not have an outdoor patio.

All travelers at DEN have access to the public outdoor patios at the ends of concourses A, B and C.

#6160. Pence delivers scathing rebuke of Vance's Iran war assessment, blames Trump policies for GOP losses

Former Vice President Mike Pence, in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview, disputes Vice President Vance’s take on GOP losses, points to what he calls 'self-dealing' and 'air of corruption' in Trump second term.

EXCLUSIVE - Former Vice President Mike Pence delivered a blistering assessment of Vice President JD Vance's midterm election postmortem that the war in Iran cost Republicans control of Congress, with the former vice president contending that Americans grew frustrated not because President Donald Trump launched the conflict, but because his administration failed to finish it.

Pence, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, his first following the midterms, also took aim at the vice president’s statements on Israel, saying he has "great concerns about what I’ve heard coming out of the vice president’s office with regard to Israel."

Asked about Vance's assessment, Pence said, "I disagree with the vice president about the reasons for the midterm election outcome."

"There's no question that the war in Iran became a frustration for millions of Americans, but it wasn't because President Trump started the war or took on Iran. It's because we stopped short and didn't finish it," Pence said. "As Americans saw the politics of appeasement that the administration embraced, one negotiation after another, I think people became... frustrated with the lack of progress, frustrated with the price of fuel at the pump."

RUBIO'S DEFENSE OF TRUMP'S IRAN WAR DRAWS SHARP CONTRAST WITH VANCE'S MIDTERM BLAME

But the former vice president emphasized "the reasons for this midterm election were much more complex than gasoline prices or the war in Iran. So, I respectfully disagree with my successor in that regard."

"If the world knows nothing else, the world should know that America stands with Israel. Israel is our most cherished ally. It is the only democracy in the Arab world," Pence a longtime strong supporter of Israel, emphasized.

Pence said he's "very troubled at the way that criticism of Israel on the left and on the right collapses too often into antisemitism and antisemitic rhetoric. There's no place in America for antisemitism on the left or on the right and the people that are wringing their hands about U.S. support for Israel, I get the feeling sometimes they're just using that as a thinly veiled excuse for their antisemitism."

‘HE BLAMED THE JEWS’: GOP CONGRESSMAN LEVELS EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATION AGAINST JD VANCE OVER ELECTION POSTMORTEM

Vance, in an assessment the morning after Election Day, wrote, "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night."

The vice president also cited an unnamed pollster in his X post who said voters who had abandoned the GOP wanted the administration to end the conflict, address inflation and the cost of living, put America first and change its relationship with Israel.

A Vance ally, responding to Pence's criticism, told Fox News Digital, "Former Vice President Pence had to retreat into the think tank world because his politics never developed past the Bush-era neocon warmongering that dragged us into the Middle East in the first place. He is laughably out of touch with how people feel in the real world."

VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS

Vice President JD Vance points to President Donald Trump at the Republican convention Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, in Dallas. (Alex Brandon/AP Photo)

Pence, who served as vice president in Trump's first term, pointed to the president's second term tariffs, the administration's handling of abortion medication and the first family's growing wealth as factors in the GOP's electoral defeat, arguing that Republicans must return to traditional conservative principles to reclaim their congressional majorities.

While the high cost of living and the war in Iran were key issues in the midterms, the Fox News Voter Poll also highlighted that 55% of respondents said government corruption was a "crucial" factor in their vote for Congress, with another 36% saying it was a major factor.

Pence argued that "I don't think you can ignore the air of corruption that's emerged around this administration, the self-dealing. The American people saw a First Family seeing their wealth increase by more than $3 billion including more than a billion dollars in cryptocurrency."

Asked by Fox Digital if he thought the president and his family had improperly profited from being in the White House, Pence answered, "I wouldn't have any way of knowing and wouldn't care to speculate."

"Mike Pence’s total and complete lack of courage caused untold damage to our great country," said White House spokesman Davis Ingle. "If Republican voters cared what Mike Pence had to say, he wouldn’t have had to drop out of the presidential race months before the Iowa caucuses."

The former vice president, referring to the midterm results which saw the Democrats storm back to grab a large House majority, take control of the Senate, and win a majority of the nation's governorships, said it "wasn't just a rout, it was a reckoning."

"I believe our voters rejected President Trump's redirection of our movement toward protectionist tariffs, toward policies of appeasement toward Russia and even Iran, toward marginalizing the right to life, and I think the era of corruption around the Trump administration was very concerning to millions of Americans, including our voters," Pence claimed. "I don't think the American people turned left. I think they were turned off, and that's what explains the outcome of this election."

REPUBLICANS TURN ON TRUMP AFTER DEVASTATING MIDTERM LOSSES HAND DEMOCRATS CONTROL OF CONGRESS

Looking forward, Pence said Republicans "now more than ever...need to recommit our party to the conservative principles that have defined our movement for more than 50 years."

"There's no question that the direction the president has taken our party was roundly rejected by the voters," he charged. "The key for success for the party and more importantly, the key for success for the country, is to return the Republican Party to advancing and advocating the conservative principles that have always made America strong and prosperous and free."

Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

#6159. Hyatt Hotel Promises Jonathan Adler Toiletries—But There’s Drugstore Shampoo On Its Housekeeping Cart

Hotel Avante in Mountain View, California advertises Jonathan Adler bath amenities. A reader photographed its housekeeping cart with a retail bottle of HASK shampoo resting among unbranded squeeze bottles. This is another JdV by Hyatt property, just a few miles from the Wild Palms hotel where I reported on DRIFT bulk toiletries on housekeeping carts while the guest bathroom bottles displayed Jonathan Adler branding. Apparently readers need to keep checking what’s on the carts. The brown bottle is HASK Tea Tree Oil & Rosemary Invigorating Shampoo, in the 12-ounce size. HASK is an affordable retail hair care brand, with products sold at CVS and other stores. Around it are condiment-style squeeze bottles. At least one has “Body wash” handwritten on tape. That identifies the type of product, without telling guests whose product it is. It seems like Hyatt a good reason to check what this hotel is using to refill its toiletries. But they had this reason at its sister property, too. There needs to be much stronger monitoring. Hyatt’s Hotel Avante page lists “Jonathan Adler bath amenities” across all six room categories. The hotel’s separate website promises that as well. I have no particular opinion on HASK shampoo. My issue is that a hotel should deliver the product they specifically advertise to guests. And if the bulk toiletries in the room say they’re a specific brand, they should be that brand. The reader describes Avante as Wild Palms’ sister property and they’re both part of the same ownership group. In November 2025, I published a reader’s photos from Wild Palms. The bathroom had Jonathan Adler bottles, while the housekeeping cart carried large jugs of DRIFT Hydrated Body Care. Then in January, Ben at One Mile at a Time published follow-up photos showing the bulk jugs with their labels removed. Wild Palms still advertises Jonathan Adler toiletries. I just wrote about the ketchup, mustard and mayonnaise bottle approach to hotel toiletries. Once the hotel keeps reusing the branded packaging, it can change the contents without changing anything the guest sees. An owner who substitutes a cheaper product keeps the savings, while Hyatt and the advertised toiletry company risk their reputations. Remind me again why bulk dispensers were a better idea than single use biodegradable packaging? Topics on this pageHotel AvanteHyattJonathan AdlerCaliforniaCVS Pharmacy+2 more More From View from the Wing

I have no particular opinion on HASK shampoo. My issue is that a hotel should deliver the product they specifically advertise to guests. And if the bulk toiletries in the room say they’re a specific brand, they should be that brand.

The reader describes Avante as Wild Palms’ sister property and they’re both part of the same ownership group. In November 2025, I published a reader’s photos from Wild Palms. The bathroom had Jonathan Adler bottles, while the housekeeping cart carried large jugs of DRIFT Hydrated Body Care.

I understand the dismay of false advertising but does anyone really pick a hotel based on the shampoo or soap offered vs loyalty points, location, free/discounted parking and breakfast, and location? I’m seriously interested.

@Ray: Pretty much any legitimate brand of shampoo would be acceptable to me, but I still don’t find it acceptable to advertise one brand and refill the bottles with a different brand.

If the shampoo bottles in the shower were labeled Suave, and we saw bulk bottles of Suave on the housekeepers’ carts (in the original packaging from Unilever, not bottles with handwritten labels on tape), that would give me more confidence with regard to the hotel’s shampoo policy than what this Hyatt is doing.

It wasn’t. I have some sympathy for the environmental argument for the re-usable bottles, but corporate culture in the US showing [again] that they will take advantage of anything they can to save a buck. The bulk bottles on the wall were never a good idea, if for no other reason than hygene (who thinks they replace these once a year, if at all). But this is another reason. Taking advantage of customers, even at ‘luxury’ properties. Makes me wonder if we overvalue hotels and should just go straight to Fairfield Inn.

And these are just the instances we know about. If there are confirmed sightings of this in the past couple of months, imagine the actual scope of the problem, I assume this is going on at thousands of hotels.

If I were at Jonathan Adler, I’d start off by suing Hyatt for false marketing (or legal equivalent). For us guests, seems like it’s time to start pushing legislation that will force compliance. Require unopened, personal-size bottles of toiletries in every room. I have no problem with requiring it to be biodegradable, but even without this, seems reasonable from a hygiene standpoint. Even anllowing accurately labeled [bulk] bottles might be a slippery slope – if hotels have openly flouted that by using ‘ketchup’ bottles to refill, I imagine their reaction to comply might be to buy a single bulk bottle of advertised brand for each cart, then keep refilling that with the cheap sub.

On the other hand, maybe hotels would just revolt and stop providing these toiletries as amenities. As a traveller, might be a PITA to bring my own, but preferable to what seems to be going on now.

It all comes out of the same large industrial drum in the basement labeled “Universal Cleaner Base – 200 L – Made in China.”

@Emcampbe and others: It was NEVER about the environment. Never. It was ALWAYS about thinking of a way they could market sh*t and get people to accept it — even praise them for it.

We’ve seen that very thing in comments on in these forums: Person A complains about this sort of con-job, and Person B comes back with, “Hey, at least they’re trying to save the planet.”

I fully agree with @Emcampbe that the first step should be for Adler to sue them, arguing Hyatt is knowingly damaging their brand by passing off inferior products as theirs. If the neighborhood Piggly Wiggly starting putting name brand labels on cheap generics it would be an easy lawsuit. This is no different.

Why would a libertarian law professor have a toiletry brand?

One real issue here is that I have allergies to some brands and if they were substituted in and I didn’t know, my skin might break out.

I agree that the switch isn’t a good look. I just feel like is no benefit in advertising a brand. Just list shampoo supplied.

Of the chains, Hyatt properties are the most egregious offenders of using condiment-style bottles to squeeze unknown products into dispensers that are never cleaned or sanitized. I’ve even seen this at Grand Hyatt properties.

I think it’s high time the elites are forced to use these low-quality products.

I’m not a shampoo snob, I don’t have enough hair to be one but this can cause some real problems for people with alleges.

Some are allergic/ sensitive to tea tree oil. I bring my own products because I don’t want to worry about a reaction away from home. Most will never have an issue.

@Ray Not the shampoo itself, but if a hotel quietly swaps what it advertises I’d wonder what else on the listing is loose. For the stuff you mention I compare the full stay, room plus parking and breakfast, not the headline rate. FWIW free tools like Arbitrica or similar check the same hotel from a bunch of countries to find kind of the lowest price in the world, since rates and inventory differ by country. Then let location decide

@Matt — You know what would solve this… better consumer protections… *wink*

@Maryland — Tried to mention to you earlier this week, I finally made it to western PA. Thank you again for recommending.

1990 great. Snow moving in any time. So many acres. So sad. I cry thinking about it

No one who travels likes the large bottles in the shower. Who knows what people put into them. I travel with my own soap etc. I don’t want any surprises.

@RT – I’ve known Jonathan for 30 years, and he never mentioned it to me! 😉

There are real working solutions already employed by other industries for this problem that keep operators honest while still allowing multi use containers. Welcome to the stage Heinz ketchup.

That company that figured it all out and have pretty successfully stopped every trick in the book by restaurants trying to get away with refilling Heinz bottles with cheaper crappier products.

They do things like: – Sell large multi use bottles to restaurants but do not allowing refilling in their contracts, they must be replaced. – they have created dispenser systems that can only be refilled by replacing internal sealed bags that cant be refilled (those big Heinz branded condiment boxes you use the pump handle to get ketchup out of). – They give restaurants Heinz bottles that are always transparent and the label has a red outline around the ages that is perfectly color matched with Heinz ketchup so is largely invisible when filled with Heinz ketchup but sticks out clearly when the bottle is full of a different brand’s ketchup. – And most of all they aggressively audit restaurants and sue if they find violations. – Probably way more tricks of the trade then that too.

The toiletry brands should employ some of the same techniques with hotels, they are not that hard. As long as the hotel is not lying about it and keeping them sanitized I actually like the user experience of larger multi use products as I like liquid soap better then bars and you don’t run out if your sharing a room with another person.

@Maryland — It was so well-done. Lost it at the ‘tower of voices’… windy day; it was like they were singing. And how they included the child for Ms. Grancolas. The answering machines. Wow. (Winter isn’t all bad; would like to return, someday, maybe see Fallingwater in the snow.) Take care out there.

Love it. Hard core political discussions (vs. travel discussions) to shampoo snobbery.. A real eclectic site.

I was at the tower of voices before the actual opening. The place is spiritual. And falling water. Is part of my history. Try the Nemacolin resort nearby for an awesome array of summer activity. Who doesn’t want to drive hummers over rocks and shoot guns? Maggie also has another less expensive hotel nearby . They filmed that bachelor series there if you are looking for a date….always. Maryland

@Maryland — Aww! It really is. There was a school group when I was there; reminded me that these kids weren’t even alive when it happened. All sorts of ‘feels.’ Taking notes for next time. Saw a car with Maryland plates and a cute bumper sticker with “tell your dog I said hi” (Thought of you! Unlike Matthew, I love dogs…Bah!)

@Quinn…agreeed. If I was a brand promoted on the bottle and my product wasn’t in there, I’d sue them for sure. As someone mentioned, some people have allergies to specific ingredients. Not that the ingredients are necessarily on the labels in hotels, but those people probably have a good idea what brands to steer clear of. Would be great for someone to have a reaction, sue the product manufacturer and then find out it wasn’t their product.

All about the chip, chip, chip to keep increasing profits.
